questions.text:
A school science fair has a water wave demonstration. A long tank has one shallow end and one deep end. Waves move from left to right.

Name the physics phenomenon that causes changes in the waves as they move from deep to shallow water.

Waves are generated at 8 waves in 10.0 seconds. The initial wavelength is 5.0 cm, reducing to 3.0 cm at the shallow end.

Calculate the final velocity of the waves at the shallow end.
questions.expectedAnswer: f = 8/10 = 0.80 Hz. v_deep = f x lambda_deep = 0.80 x 0.050 = 0.040 m/s. v_shallow/v_deep = lambda_shallow/lambda_deep. v_shallow = 0.040 x 0.030/0.050 = 0.024 m/s.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correct frequency. Merit: Correct velocity.

questions.text:
Describe and explain the phenomenon identified in part (a), as the wave moves from deep to shallow water.

Include changes to wavelength, velocity, amplitude, and frequency.
questions.expectedAnswer: The wave slows down as it enters shallow water. Wavelength decreases proportionally. Frequency remains constant (set by the source). Amplitude may increase slightly as energy is concentrated in a slower, shorter wave.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: TWO correct points. Merit: THREE linked. Excellence: All FOUR.

questions.text:
A demonstration rope consists of a less dense rope joined to a more dense rope. A student sends a pulse from left to right along the less dense rope.

Complete the diagram to show both the transmitted and reflected pulse after the pulse hits the boundary.

Label the transmitted and reflected pulses.
questions.expectedAnswer: Reflected pulse: opposite phase (inverted), smaller amplitude, further from boundary. Transmitted pulse: same phase (upright), smaller amplitude, closer to boundary and slower.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Any correct feature. Merit: THREE features. Excellence: Fully correct diagram.

questions.text: Compare the velocity of the reflected pulse with that of the transmitted pulse.
questions.expectedAnswer: The reflected pulse is faster than the transmitted pulse (it travels in the less dense rope).

questions.text:
A room has curved mirrors. Hemi looks into a large curved mirror. His reflection is enlarged and upright.

State the third property of the image.

Hemi is 1.7 m tall and stands 0.80 m in front of the mirror, which has a focal length of 1.5 m.

Calculate the height of the image.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correct di. Merit: Correct hi.

questions.text:
Hemi stands 3.0 m in front of a concave mirror with focal length 1.5 m.

Complete a ray diagram to locate the image.
questions.expectedAnswer: Image is inverted, real, same size as object, located at di = 3.0 m (= 2f).
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correct image nature. Merit: Correct ray diagram. Excellence: Ray diagram with image described.

questions.text: State the three properties of the image formed.
questions.expectedAnswer: Inverted, real, same size as object.

questions.text:
A candle is placed in front of a convex lens. The image is inverted and diminished.

State the property that allows the image to be projected on a screen.
Complete a ray diagram to show how the inverted and diminished image is formed.
questions.expectedAnswer: Object placed beyond 2F, two correct rays drawn, image between F and 2F on other side, inverted and diminished.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: One correct ray. Merit: Two rays. Excellence: Complete diagram.

questions.text:
The students move the candle to produce a larger image, still able to be formed on a screen.

Explain how the image size can be made larger.
questions.expectedAnswer: Move the candle closer to the lens (but keep it beyond F so the image remains real).

questions.text:
The final display uses fibre optics. A fibre optic cable has a glass core within a cladding.

State what n1 and n2 represent.
questions.expectedAnswer: Refractive indices (of the core and cladding materials).

questions.text: Name the phenomenon that allows light to be transmitted along the fibre optic cable.
State the conditions required for this phenomenon within the fibre optic cable.
questions.expectedAnswer: The angle of incidence on the core-cladding boundary must be greater than the critical angle, and light must travel from the denser medium (core) to the less dense medium (cladding).
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: One condition. Merit: Both conditions in context.

questions.text:
A beam of light shines through a tank filled with glycerine. The light moves from glycerine into air.

Add a labelled arrow to show the refracted ray.
questions.expectedAnswer: Ray bending away from normal in air, with label and arrow.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correct direction. Merit: Correct with angle.

questions.text:
The angle of incidence on the glycerine-air boundary is 25 degrees.
Refractive index of air = 1.00.
Speed of light in air: v1 = 3.00 x 10^8 m s-1
Speed in glycerine: v2 = 2.04 x 10^8 m s-1

Calculate the angle of refraction in air.
questions.expectedAnswer: n_glycerine = v_air/v_glycerine = 3.00e8/2.04e8 = 1.47. n1 sin theta1 = n2 sin theta2. 1.47 x sin 25 = 1.00 x sin theta2. sin theta2 = 0.621. theta2 = 38.4 degrees.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: n found or correct direction. Merit: Two of three correct. Excellence: Correct angle.

questions.text:
As visitors leave, they pass two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator, both producing the same frequency at the same volume.

Describe and explain changes to the sound experienced as people walk past.
questions.expectedAnswer: Visitors hear alternating loud and soft sounds due to constructive and destructive interference. Where path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, constructive interference occurs (loud). Where path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths, destructive interference occurs (soft).
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: ONE point. Merit: THREE points. Excellence: Full explanation with path difference.
